text: Part three · what touch does

title: Three · what touch does
section: Touch turns pain down, and company turns it down further
text:
Touch turns pain down, and company turns it down further

1965 onward


The oldest practical claim about touch, and one of the better supported. Rubbing a banged elbow is not superstition; there is a mechanism, and it was proposed sixty years ago.


The research Melzack & Wall’s gate control theory (1965)1, then Coan, Schaefer & Davidson (2006)2 and Goldstein and colleagues (2018)3. The framework is one of the field’s starting points, and much revised since; the handholding studies are small and replicated in direction.


The original 1965 drawing, much simplified. Sixty years of revision have complicated the mechanism without overturning the central claim.

The idea was that pain signals have to pass through a gate in the spinal cord on their way up, and that fast touch fibres arriving from the same patch of skin can partly close it. Signals coming down from the brain — attention, expectation, mood — can open or close it too.
The details have been revised many times in sixty years. The central claim has held: touch and pain are not independent channels, and one turns the other up or down before either reaches awareness.
Then there is who is doing the touching. When women anticipating an electric shock held someone’s hand, the threat response in the brain was reduced — less by a stranger’s hand than by their husband’s, and the better they rated the marriage, the larger the effect. Later work found that handholding during pain came with increased coupling between the two people’s brain activity, and that the more empathic the partner, the more the pain went down.

For your hands Contact can genuinely reduce pain, and it is not only about the contact — the same hand does more when it belongs to someone the person trusts. That is an argument for the relationship being part of the treatment rather than around it.

title: Three · what touch does
section: Everyone carries a map of who may touch them where
text:
Everyone carries a map of who may touch them where

2015


Not a metaphor either. Ask people to shade in which parts of their body a given person is allowed to touch, and something very orderly comes out.


The research Suvilehto and colleagues (2015)4. Large and cross-cultural, and entirely self-report — maps of what people say they would allow, which is not the same as what happens.


The zones are a simplification of the published maps; the area-against-bond relationship on the right is the paper’s actual finding.

1,368 people across five countries did exactly that, for everyone from a partner to a stranger. The maps were remarkably consistent, and the headline finding is almost embarrassingly simple: the total area a person is allowed to touch tracks the strength of the emotional bond. Cultural differences were minor.
Hands are permitted to nearly everyone. The area expands outward from there as the relationship closes, and for a stranger most of the body is off limits. The regions people guard most closely are also the regions they rate as most pleasurable to be touched on.
You occupy an unusual position on that map. As a practitioner you are given access it reserves for the people we are closest to — by agreement, in a role, for a purpose. That is a real thing to hold carefully, and it is why consent in this work is not a formality.

For your hands Your hands are on territory that, for this person, is normally reserved. Saying what you are about to do before you do it is not politeness. It is how the map gets redrawn safely.

title: Three · what touch does
section: How sure can we be about any of this?
text:
How sure can we be about any of this?

The evidence


Touch research makes a lot of claims and they are not equally supported. Here they are sorted honestly, because the strong ones get less airtime than the shaky ones.


The research This one figure is a judgement rather than any single paper’s result — a reading of the literature cited throughout, leaning on Kidd, Devine & Walker’s review5 for the stress claims and Moyer and colleagues’ meta-analysis6 for the cortisol one.


Positions are a judgement about how much weight to give each claim, not measured effect sizes. Arranged so the shape of the field is visible.

Notice the shape of it. The best-supported claims are the simplest and most physical: contact reduces pain, skin-to-skin contact steadies newborns. The weakest are the ones about hormones — the oxytocin and cortisol stories that circulate most confidently in training rooms are the ones the evidence supports least well.
That is not an accident. Subjective outcomes are easy to measure and to move; blood hormones are hard to measure, vary enormously between people and across a day, and rarely shift as neatly as the story requires. When you hear a claim about touch and a named hormone, treat it as the least secure thing in the sentence.

For your hands You do not need the hormone claims. The evidence you actually have — pain, comfort, distress, sleep in newborns — is stronger, more directly about what people come to you for, and much harder to argue with.

title: Two · the second system
text: Part two · the second system

title: Two · the second system
section: Someone put a needle in a nerve and listened
text:
Someone put a needle in a nerve and listened

1999


The second road was found by a group in Gothenburg who were not looking for it. The technique is microneurography, and it is exactly as unlikely as it sounds: a very fine electrode placed into a nerve in a fully awake person, listening to single fibres while their skin is touched.


The research Vallbo, Olausson & Wessberg (1999)1. Not disputed — this is the discovery, and it has held for twenty-five years.


The spike patterns are drawn to show the idea, not measured. The contrast is the real one: these fibres were told apart from pain fibres precisely by answering a gentle stimulus and not a sharp one.

Recording from forearm skin, they kept finding fibres that made no sense. They were unmyelinated — the thin, slow kind everyone associated with pain and temperature — but they responded happily to a soft brush, and hardly at all to anything sharp.
Of 38 units they picked for answering to gentle pressure on the skin, 27 were this low-threshold kind. That ratio is not a count of how common they are — the units were chosen for responding to light touch in the first place. What tells you these fibres are not rare is a separate observation: the team reported running into them about as often as the classic fast ones.
The title of the paper is the whole finding: unmyelinated fibres make up a second system for coding touch in human hairy skin. What it was doing there was completely open.

For your hands These fibres are called CT afferents — C for the slow, unmyelinated kind — the ones with no insulating sheath — and T for touch. That is the term you will meet everywhere else, and this is where it comes from.

title: Two · the second system
section: The man who could not feel touch, and felt it anyway
text:
The man who could not feel touch, and felt it anyway

2002


A second system is a nice idea, but how would you ever separate it from the first? The answer arrived in the form of a patient who had lost the fast road entirely.


The research Olausson and colleagues (2002)2. Strong evidence, and a single case — you cannot arrange for a second patient.




A rare nerve disease had destroyed his large, insulated fibres. On any standard test he had no sense of touch on his body: he could not feel a poke, could not say where he had been touched, could not feel vibration. The fast road was gone.
Then they stroked his forearm softly with a brush. He felt something — faint, hard to locate, and pleasant. And when they scanned his brain, the signal was not arriving at the usual place. It was lighting up the insula, a region that deals with how the body feels from the inside: hunger, warmth, breath, discomfort.
This is the study that turned an anatomical curiosity into a claim about experience. The slow road does not just exist. It goes somewhere different, and somewhere with more in common with emotion than with the map of your skin.

For your hands Affectionate touch is not a gentler version of informative touch. On this evidence it takes a different road and arrives somewhere else in the brain.

title: Two · the second system
section: And it has a favourite speed
text:
And it has a favourite speed

2009


If these fibres were built for being stroked, you would expect them to care about how fast. They do — and it is not the fastest, and it is not the slowest.


The research Löken and colleagues (2009)3. Widely replicated as a group average; individuals vary more than the tidy curve suggests, which part four returns to.


Curve shapes follow the published figure; the firing values are rough rather than exact. The dot moves at the real speed.

They brushed people’s forearms at five speeds while listening to single fibres, then asked how pleasant each stroke felt. The fast fibres did the sensible thing: the quicker the brush, the harder they fired. Speed in, speed out.
The slow fibres did something more interesting. They fired hardest at middling speeds, around one to ten centimetres a second, and less at both extremes. Drag the dial and watch the shape. It is a hill, not a ramp.
And how pleasant people rated it made the same hill. The speeds that lit up these fibres were the speeds people liked, and this range is often described as the speed of a caress. Worth a caveat that is easy to lose: when spontaneous stroking has actually been measured, it tends to run somewhat faster than the tuning peak, even though people stroke more slowly the closer they feel to the person. The hill is real. “This is exactly how humans naturally caress” is a tidier story than the measurements support.

For your hands The dot moves at the real speed. Watch it rather than the curve, then try matching it with your own hand on your forearm. That is what the research is describing.

title: Two · the second system
section: It also wants you to be warm
text:
It also wants you to be warm

2014


A second tuning, and the one most likely to change what you actually do. These fibres are fussy about temperature, and the temperature they want is skin.


The research Ackerley and colleagues (2014)4. Well supported, and a small study — as all microneurography is.


A simplified picture of two findings held together. The sweet spot is drawn as a region because that is how it behaves, not as a measured contour.

They repeated the stroking experiment at different temperatures. The fibres responded best to a brush at about 32 degrees — neutral skin temperature. Not warm. Not cool. The temperature of another person.
And the ratings followed. People found every speed more pleasant at skin temperature than at 18 degrees or at 42 degrees. Get the warmth wrong and the speed cannot rescue it.
Try the two together in the panel. The sweet spot is a small region, not a line, and both dimensions have to be right to land in it.

For your hands Cold hands are not merely unpleasant, they are the wrong stimulus. So is oil straight from a cool bottle, and so is a treatment room a couple of degrees under. This is the cheapest change on this page.

title: What we carry back into the room
text: Closing

title: What we carry back into the room
section: What we would carry back into the room
text:
What we would carry back into the room

In practice


Ten things we came away with, loosely ordered by how much weight we would put on each.



Slower than feels natural — about a hand’s width a second.
One to ten centimetres a second is where the research clusters, and it is slower than most of us work by default.
Warmth seems to matter about as much as speed.
Around skin temperature — hands, oil, room. Cold shifted every speed toward less pleasant, and technique did not appear to make up for it.
Hairy skin looks like the home ground, though not the only ground.
Forearm, back, shoulders. The palm has some of these fibres after all — just fewer.
Still contact seems to count.
Resting a hand is not a lesser version of stroking. It may be preferred to stroking done wrong.
What you are trying to do decides which system you are working with.
Fine detail comes through a fingertip on hairless skin. Contact and comfort come through a broad, slow, warm hand on hairy skin.
Averages describe populations, not the person on the table.
The curve is an average across a lot of people. We would ask, watch and adjust rather than put a number on someone.
Saying what you are about to do matters more than we expected.
You have access the social map normally saves for the people we are closest to. Saying it out loud seems to be how that stays safe rather than just allowed.
Describing the touch travels further than describing the mechanism.
“Slow, warm, light, moving” is honest and checkable. “Activating your C-tactile fibres” goes beyond the evidence.
The hormone claims are the ones we would hold most loosely.
That evidence is the thinnest thing here. The pain and comfort findings are steadier and need no help from it.
Most of the work is probably not being done by the fibres.
Safety, consent, predictability and relationship. The fibres are the doorway, not the visit.

title: What we carry back into the room
section: If you want to go further
text:
If you want to go further

Reading


Four places to go next, in the order we would send someone.


McGlone et al. (2014) — The standard overview, free to read, and the source most people are quoting second-hand. Long, but the first half is very approachable.
Morrison et al. (2010) — The friendliest conceptual framing of why any of this might matter.
Kidd et al. (2023) — The bridge from nerve fibres to stress physiology, and the closest thing to a review written for people who do this for a living.
Suvilehto et al. (2023) — The widest recent view — who touches whom, where, and what for.


Assembled in 2026 from the literature as it stood. A reading of published research, written for people who work with touch. It is not medical advice, it does not describe a technique, and it cannot tell you what the person in front of you wants. Where researchers disagree we have tried to say so rather than tidy it away — that is not hedging, it is the current state of a young field still arguing productively with itself.


Every source the journey cites, in the order it cites them. Each page also carries its own references at the foot, numbered for that page.

title: Four · being honest about it
text: Part four · being honest about it

title: Four · being honest about it
section: Four things this field has had to take back
text:
Four things this field has had to take back

2012–2023


Everything in part two is a decade old or more, and parts of it have been revised. A practitioner quoting the 2014 version is now quoting something the researchers have moved on from.


The research Six papers between 2021 and 2023, named on the cards: Watkins1, Case2, Ali3, Bendas4, Crucianelli5 and — the largest — Schirmer, Croy & Ackerley6, a review by researchers inside the field checking their own published work.


Four corrections from the last decade. Tap each card to turn it over.

None of these demolish the story. They complicate it in ways that mostly make it more useful, and they are worth knowing so that you are not the last person in the room still saying the old version.
The fourth is the largest and the least comfortable. Going through the literature, the authors found that of the papers using the phrase “affective touch”, only 34% even mention these fibres. A nerve fibre and a human experience had quietly become the same word, and they are not the same thing.

For your hands When you explain your work, describe the touch — slow, light, warm, moving, on a forearm — rather than claiming to activate a named nerve fibre. The first is accurate and checkable; the second goes further than anyone can currently support.

title: Four · being honest about it
section: The fibre is not the feeling
text:
The fibre is not the feeling

Now


The most useful correction of all, and it comes from within the research rather than from its critics.


The research Sailer & Leknes (2022)7 and Schirmer, Croy & Schweinberger (2022)8. Position pieces rather than experiments — arguments about how to read the evidence, from people who generated much of it.


Illustrative, not measured — no study assigns these labels. It is here because the point is hard to feel from a sentence and easy to feel from a switch.

The same stroke, at the same speed and the same temperature, is not the same experience depending on who is doing it, whether you consented, what happened last time, and what you believe it is for. One paper’s title puts it plainly: meaning makes touch affective. The other argues that social touch is better understood as a tool people use to do something to each other than as a signal being transmitted.
That is not a demotion of the nerve fibres. It is a description of where they sit. They look like a doorway — a channel well suited to carrying this kind of contact. What comes through the doorway is decided by everything else.
Which is, if you think about it, what a good practitioner already knows. The biology has caught up with the room.

For your hands Speed and warmth are worth getting right, and they are the smaller half. Consent, predictability, and whether the person wanted to be touched by you are doing more work than any number on this page.

title: Touch is not one sense
text:
A reading journey for hands-on practitioners



Skin carries at least two separate systems, and they are not sending the same message. One tells you what you are touching. The other answers mainly to being touched affectionately — found by accident, confirmed by a man who had lost the ordinary sense of touch, and it fires hardest at one particular speed. What follows is what we found reading our way through it: what each system responds to, what touch does to pain and to relationships, and which of the popular claims we could not get to stand up.

title: Touch is not one sense
text:
The four parts
The journey runs in order, and each part builds on the one before it. Every page carries its own references at the foot.

One · the territory — two roads, the receptors they arrive on, and how finely skin can actually resolve what it feels.
Two · the second system — how the slow road was found, the patient who proved it carries an experience, and the two things it is tuned to.
Three · what touch does — pain, the map of who may touch you where, and an honest sorting of how sure anyone can be about any of it.
Four · being honest about it — four things the field has had to take back, and why the fibre is not the feeling.
What we carry back into the room — ten things we came away with, further reading, and the complete reference list.


Assembled in 2026 from the literature as it stood. A reading of published research, written for people who work with touch. It is not medical advice, it does not describe a technique, and it cannot tell you what the person in front of you wants.

title: One · the territory
text: Part one · the territory

title: One · the territory
section: There are two ways of being touched
text:
There are two ways of being touched

The idea


Everything else here follows from one thing: touch is not a single sense. Two separate kinds of nerve fibre leave the skin at the same instant, travelling at very different speeds, and they are not carrying the same message.


The research This first stop is the shared framework rather than a single study — it is drawn from the review by McGlone, Wessberg & Olausson (2014)1, which is also the best single thing to read after this page.


The animation runs in real time. A fast signal crosses in a few hundredths of a second; the slow one takes about a second. That gap is the finding itself, not an effect added to illustrate it.

The fast road is the one most people mean by touch. Thick fibres wrapped in myelin, an insulating sheath that lets a signal race along at tens of metres per second. They are superb at what and where — the exact spot, the texture, the pressure, the edge of the object in your hand. This is the system that lets you find a coin in your pocket without looking.
The slow road is the surprise. Thin fibres with no insulation, a signal ambling along at about one metre per second — so slow that when someone strokes your forearm, that part of the message arrives something like a second behind the rest. They are poor at what and where. What they seem to carry, instead, is how it feels.
Those two colours — blue for the fast road, clay for the slow one — mean the same thing in every figure from here on. Nothing below assumes you have met any of this before.

For your hands If you have ever wondered why a client goes quiet a beat after your hands land rather than as they land, there is a real signal running about a second behind the obvious one.

title: One · the territory
section: You are working on a sense organ, not a covering
text:
You are working on a sense organ, not a covering

Where it happens


Skin is usually described as a barrier. It is also the largest sensory surface you have, and the fast road alone arrives on four different kinds of receptor, each answering to something different.


The research Standard anatomy rather than a finding2 — the classification of mechanoreceptors below is textbook material, and each type links to its Wikipedia entry if you want the detail.


Depths and shapes are schematic. Tap a receptor to read what it does.

Tap any receptor in the diagram. Two live near the surface and handle fine, quick things: Merkel cells for edges and texture, and Meissner corpuscles for slip — the receptor that tells you a glass is sliding out of your grip before you consciously notice.
Two sit deeper and handle slower, coarser things. Ruffini endings register stretch across the skin, part of how you know where your hand is without looking. Pacinian corpuscles register fast vibration, which is how you feel the texture of a surface through the end of a tool rather than through your fingertips.
And then the fifth kind: bare nerve endings with no capsule at all, wandering in the hairy skin. Those are the slow road, and the next four stops are about them.

For your hands When you change from a fingertip to a flat palm, from gliding to holding, from still to vibrating, you are not adjusting an intensity. You are moving between different receptors with different jobs.

title: One · the territory
section: Your fingertips are twenty times sharper than your back
text:
Your fingertips are twenty times sharper than your back

How fine


How close together can two points be before skin stops feeling them as two? The answer varies across the body by more than twenty-fold — and the conclusion people usually draw from that is wider than the measurement allows.


The research The numbers everyone quotes come from Weinstein’s 1968 survey3. The test itself has been questioned for years as a measure of how finely you can feel4 — the ranking across the body is solid, the exact millimetres softer than they look.


Drawn larger than life so the smallest gaps stay visible; the proportions between body parts are the real ones. Values are the classic Weinstein figures, widely reproduced — the ranking is solid, the exact millimetres less so.

Pick a body part and look at the gap drawn to scale. On a fingertip the two dots have to come within two or three millimetres before they merge into one. On the back they can be nearly four centimetres apart and still feel like a single touch. This is two-point discrimination, and it tracks how densely the fast receptors are packed.
It is tempting to conclude from this that precision on a back is pointless. That would be over-reading a very narrow measurement, in at least three ways. Locating a single contact is generally more accurate than telling two apart, so a person can often say roughly where your hand is even where they could not resolve two touches. Pressure reaches past the skin — muscle, fascia and joints have their own sensory supply, and where you press changes what you are pressing on whatever the skin can resolve. And the precision may matter most to you: feeling your way is information travelling to you, the practitioner, and your fingertips resolve at two or three millimetres.
What the number does tell you is narrower and still worth having: do not expect fine surface detail on a back to be perceived as detail by the person receiving it. And treat the exact figures gently — people can sometimes report “two” when both points are in the same place, which suggests the task picks up cues besides spacing.

For your hands Try it on yourself with two pencil tips or a bent paperclip. Fingertip, forearm, back. Then have someone touch one spot on your back and point to where you think it was — you will usually be closer than the two-point figure would suggest.
